issues.legal_issue: A mining lease cannot be extended for a period during which operations were obstructed when no statute or lease term grants that extension and the prevailing mining policy requires new leases to be granted through a competitive process.
material_facts: Mining operations under the leases were stopped following an order made in proceedings in which the leaseholders had not been joined.
The interruption was not attributable to the leaseholders, and the lands covered by their leases were ultimately excluded from the relevant forest area.
The lease terms and the applicable statutory rules did not provide a right to extend the leases for the obstructed period.
The mining policy in force when an extension would have to be granted required leases to be granted through e-tendering or e-auction.
The State had agreed to refund relevant security deposits and advance royalties.
issues.conclusion: The leases should not be extended for the obstructed period. The applicable rules provide for monetary adjustment of amounts paid for a period when mining could not take place, rather than an extension of the lease.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Uttar Pradesh Mining Minerals (Concession) Rules, 1963, Rule 68 is a restricted relaxation power to be read with the rules governing grants and auctions; it does not create a right to extend an expired lease to compensate for an interruption. A right to extension must arise from statute or the lease terms. Rule 40(h) provides for adjustment of the installment equivalent to the disrupted period. The Court relied on Sukhan Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Mohammad Yunus Hasan v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Vijay Kumar Dwivedi v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and applied the principle that clear statutory language is given its literal meaning. The prevailing mining policy requiring competitive allocation also weighed against extension.

rule.if: mining_lease_appeal and mining_operations_obstructed and no_lessee_fault and (not statutory_extension_right and not contractual_extension_right) and prevailing_policy_requires_competitive_grant

predicates.mining_lease_appeal: A leaseholder appeals in a proceeding concerning the consequences of an interruption to mining under a mining lease.
predicates.mining_operations_obstructed: Mining operations under the lease were prevented for a period by an order or other restriction.
predicates.no_lessee_fault: The interruption was not caused by wrongdoing or fault of the leaseholder.
predicates.statutory_extension_right: A statute gives the leaseholder a right to extend the lease for the obstructed period.
predicates.contractual_extension_right: The lease terms give the leaseholder a right to extend the lease for the obstructed period.
predicates.prevailing_policy_requires_competitive_g: The policy in force when a new grant or extension would be made requires mining rights to be allocated through a competitive process.
predicates.obstructed_lease_extension_denied: The lease is not extended for the obstructed period.

issues.definition: When a leaseholder appeals after mining operations were obstructed without the leaseholder's fault, and neither statute nor contract provides an extension right while the prevailing policy requires competitive grants, the lease is not extended for the obstructed period.

issues.legal_issue: When mining operations are obstructed without fault of the leaseholder and amounts have been paid for the affected period, refund of those amounts may be accompanied by interest to do complete justice.
material_facts: The leaseholders' mining operations were prevented for a period without fault on their part.
The leaseholders had paid security deposits and advance royalties, including amounts relating to the period when they could not operate.
The State agreed to refund the relevant security deposits and advance royalties.
The rules provided for monetary adjustment for disruption but did not provide for an extension of the leases or compensation for the broader losses claimed.
The leaseholders' money remained blocked while mining was prevented.
issues.conclusion: The Court directed refund of any unreturned security deposits and advance royalties, together with simple interest at 9% per annum. It used its power under Article 142 to award interest, but did not grant the requested lease extensions.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 40(h) of the Uttar Pradesh Mining Minerals (Concession) Rules, 1963 provides for adjustment of the amount equivalent to installments payable during a disrupted period. Exercising its power under Article 142 of the Constitution to do complete justice, the Court awarded simple interest on the refundable amounts because the leaseholders' money had remained blocked and the interruption was not their fault. The Court considered the ordinary principle in Beg Raj Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh that a successful party should, so far as appropriate, be restored to the position it would have occupied absent the wrong, while holding that this principle did not justify overriding the statutory framework and prevailing policy to extend leases.

rule.if: mining_lease_appeal and mining_operations_obstructed and no_lessee_fault and (unreturned_security_deposit or advance_royalty_for_interrupted_period)
